newsitem.title: GERMANY: German union urges "ordered retreat" on shop hours.
newsitem.headline: German union urges "ordered retreat" on shop hours.

text.p: German retail trade union HBV on Wednesday urged employers who were not benefiting from relaxed shop opening laws to make an "ordered retreat" towards the old shopping hours.
It backed up its demand by publishing a survey indicating that the new hours, introduced last November, had boosted neither retail jobs nor overall sales in the sector.

Representatives of retail employers reluctantly accepted that this was the case. But they said international comparisons showed that German opening hours, among the most rigid in Europe, had been desperately in need of reform.

HBV said that shops had faced higher costs in introducing the new hours but overall retail revenues had fallen over the five months since their introduction. Working conditions for retail staff had meanwhile worsened, it added.

"Those employers clearly deriving no benefit from the longer hours should immediately organise an ordered retreat. Commercial sense and responsibilty to employees must finally take precedence," HBV retail expert Franziska Wiethold said in a statment.
HBV said its findings were based on information from work councils representing the some 2.6 million employees in the retail sector.
From November, German shops have been allowed to stay open until 8 pm on weekday evenings, compared with 6.30 pm before, while Saturday shopping runs a further two hours until 4 pm.
The new law was greeted by Germans with reactions ranging from enthusiasm among mainly young consumers to protests that it would lead to a disruption of family life.

Hermann Franzen, president of the German Retail Federation, confirmed that retail revenues had fallen since the new opening hours and that no jobs would be created in the industry until Germany's tentative economic recovery gained pace.

But he told German radio that advocates of longer opening hours were "not completely wrong when they say that laws on German shopping hours were, when international comparisons are drawn, in need of reform".
German opening times are still shorter than those in the rest of Europe and way behind the virtually deregulated shopping hours in the United States and Britain.
Official employment data last month showed that the longer opening hours had stemmed the steady year-on-year decline in retail jobs.
But the statistics also highlighted that this was because of a sharp increase in part-time workers and that the number of full-time jobs was still falling in the industry.
HBV's Wiethold said that stores which were determined to persist with longer opening should also increase their staff levels proportionately.
"Those employers that want to push through longer hours without more staff will damage customer service levels and the reputation of the retail sector as a whole," she said.
The extension has created divisions within the retail industry itself, with large chains mostly in favour of the move and smaller stores opposed to it.
